{{Short description|Probability theory}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Kolmogorov's two-series theorem''' is a result about the convergence of random series. It follows from [[Kolmogorov's inequality]] and is used in one proof of the [[strong law of large numbers]].

== Statement of the theorem ==

Let <math>\left( X_n \right)_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> be [[independent random variables]] with [[expected value]]s <math>\mathbf{E} \left[ X_n \right] = \mu_n</math> and [[variance]]s <math>\mathbf{Var} \left( X_n \right) = \sigma_n^2</math>, such that <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu_n</math> [[convergence of random variables|converges]] in <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sigma_n^2</math> converges in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Then <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n</math> converges in <math>\mathbb{R}</math> [[almost surely]].

== Proof ==

Assume [[WLOG]] <math>\mu_n = 0</math>. Set <math>S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N X_n</math>, and we will see that <math>\limsup_N S_N - \liminf_NS_N = 0</math> with probability 1.

For every <math>m \in \mathbb{N}</math>,
<math display="block">\limsup_{N \to \infty} S_N - \liminf_{N \to \infty} S_N = \limsup_{N \to \infty} \left( S_N - S_m \right) - \liminf_{N \to \infty} \left( S_N - S_m \right) \leq 2 \max_{k \in \mathbb{N} } \left| \sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{m+i} \right|</math>

Thus, for every <math>m \in \mathbb{N}</math> and <math>\epsilon > 0</math>,
<math display="block">\begin{align} \mathbb{P} \left( \limsup_{N \to \infty} \left( S_N - S_m \right) - \liminf_{N \to \infty} \left( S_N - S_m \right) \geq \epsilon \right) &\leq \mathbb{P} \left( 2 \max_{k \in \mathbb{N} } \left| \sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{m+i} \right| \geq \epsilon \ \right) \\ &= \mathbb{P} \left( \max_{k \in \mathbb{N} } \left| \sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{m+i} \right| \geq \frac{\epsilon}{2} \ \right) \\ &\leq \limsup_{N \to \infty} 4\epsilon^{-2} \sum_{i=m+1}^{m+N} \sigma_i^2 \\ &= 4\epsilon^{-2} \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{i=m+1}^{m+N} \sigma_i^2 \end{align}</math>

While the second inequality is due to [[Kolmogorov's inequality]].

By the assumption that <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sigma_n^2</math> converges, it follows that the last term tends to 0 when <math>m \to \infty</math>, for every arbitrary <math>\epsilon > 0</math>.
